title: Power laws in log space
objectives: Fit a power law by least squares in log space and read its exponent.

screens.title: The same factor each time
screens.prose: A family of models gets ten times larger at each step, and the loss falls each time.
screens.question: By what factor does the loss shrink with each tenfold? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Divide one loss by the one before.
Check another pair: it is the same.

feedback.correct: $0.9976 / 1.2559 \approx 0.7943$, and every step gives the same factor.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide each loss by the one before it.

byKey.diff: That is the drop, which shrinks each step. The ratio stays the same.
byKey.inv: You divided the other way: the loss shrinks, so the factor is below 1.

explain.text: A constant factor per tenfold is a **power law**: $L = aN^{-\alpha}$ with $10^{-\alpha} = 0.7943$, so $\alpha = 0.1$.

screens.title: A line in log space
screens.prose: Plot $\log_{10} L$ against $\log_{10} N$ for the four models. Slide the exponent $k$ of the line $\log_{10} L = \log_{10} 5 - k \log_{10} N$.
screens.question: Which $k$ puts the line through all four points? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Slide until the line meets every point.
Each point falls 0.1 for each step right.

feedback.correct: $k = 0.1$: the four points lie on one straight line.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Keep sliding until every point sits on the line.

byKey.one: That is where the slider started.

explain.text: At $k = 0.1$ the line passes through all four points. In log space a power law is a straight line whose slope is $-\alpha$, so fitting it means fitting a line.

screens.title: The slope is the exponent
screens.prose: Taking logs of $L = aN^{-\alpha}$ gives $\ln L = \ln a - \alpha \ln N$: a straight line in $(\ln N, \ln L)$.
screens.question: What is the slope of the line through these two points? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the change in $\log L$ by the change in $\log N$.

byKey.sign: The loss falls, so the slope is negative; the exponent is minus the slope.
byKey.drop: That is the rise. Divide by the run, 3.

explain.text: The slope is $-0.1$ in base 10 or base $e$ alike, since both axes change base together. The exponent $\alpha$ is minus the slope.

screens.title: Least squares on the logs
screens.prose: With more than two points, fit the line by least squares on $x = \ln N$, $y = \ln L$ (`regression` L1): slope $= \mathrm{cov}(x, y) / \mathrm{var}(x)$, intercept $= \bar y - \text{slope} \cdot \bar x$. For the four exact points the slope is $-0.1$.
screens.question: The fit's intercept is $\ln a$. What is $a$? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: The intercept is $\ln L$ at $\ln N = 0$.

explain.text: Exponentiate the intercept to get $a = 5$. The fitted law $L = 5N^{-0.1}$ is the one that made the points.

screens.title: Fitting noisy runs
screens.prose: Real runs scatter. The number script made 7 models from $10^6$ to $10^9$ parameters with losses $5N^{-0.1}$ times seeded noise of about 2%.
screens.question: What exponent $\alpha$ does least squares on the logs give? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: The exponent is minus the slope.
It is close to, but not exactly, 0.1.

feedback.correct: The fit gives $\alpha \approx 0.0979$ and $a \approx 4.85$, near the true 0.1 and 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Fit the logs and take minus the slope.

byKey.true: That is the exponent that made the data; the noisy points give a slightly different fit.
byKey.sign: That is the slope; the exponent is its negative.

explain.text: Noise of 2% moves the fitted exponent to 0.0979. Seven points over three decades pin the exponent to within a few per cent.

screens.title: Write the fit
screens.prose: Write `fit_power_law(N, L)`, returning $(a, \alpha)$ for $L = aN^{-\alpha}$ by least squares on natural logs, and `predict_loss(a, alpha, N)`. `NN`, `LN` hold the noisy runs.
screens.question: Write `fit_power_law` and `predict_loss`.

widget.how: Submit runs 6 hidden tests: the exact law $5N^{-0.1}$, the noisy runs, Kaplan's law, two points, and two predictions. Values within $10^{-9}$ (relative).

mutants.symptom: Fits a straight line to L against N on linear axes.
Returns the slope, which is minus the exponent.
Returns ln a instead of a.
Mixes base-10 and natural logs, so the slope is off by ln 10.

hints.text: Slope $= \mathrm{cov}(x, y)/\mathrm{var}(x)$; intercept $= \bar y - $ slope $\bar x$.

feedback.correct: Your fit recovers every planted law.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 is the exact law: $a = 5$, $\alpha = 0.1$. Fit the logs, return $e^{\text{intercept}}$ and minus the slope.

explain.text: Two logs, a line, two conversions back. The same fit reads the exponent off any scaling plot.

screens.title: A line on linear axes
screens.prose: A colleague fits a straight line to $L$ against $N$ for the four exact models, on ordinary axes, and reads its slope.
screens.question: What goes wrong?

options.text: The points are not on a line, and the largest model decides it
Nothing: any line fit gives the exponent
options.why: The exponent is the slope in log space; on linear axes the slope is a tiny number with no meaning.

options.text: The slope is too small to read but correct
options.why: It is not the exponent at all; the relation is curved on linear axes.

options.text: Only noise would make it wrong
options.why: Even exact points give the wrong answer on linear axes.

hints.text: On linear axes, three of the points sit near $N = 0$.

feedback.correct: On linear axes the curve bends, the small models bunch near 0, and the largest point controls the line.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What shape do the points make on linear axes?

byKey.fine: That is the trap. Only in log space is the law a line whose slope is $-\alpha$.

explain.text: A power law is curved on linear axes, so a line fit there answers no useful question. Take logs of both axes first.

screens.title: Kaplan's law
screens.prose: Kaplan et al. (2020) fitted $L(N) = (8.8 \times 10^{13} / N)^{0.076}$ to language models, with $N$ the non-embedding parameters.
screens.question: What does the law give at $N = 10^9$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $88{,}000^{0.076} \approx 2.3756$; each tenfold multiplies the loss by $10^{-0.076} \approx 0.8395$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide, then raise to 0.076.

byKey.neg: You inverted the ratio; the law divides $8.8 \times 10^{13}$ by $N$.

explain.text: 2.8300, 2.3756, 1.9943: each tenfold multiplies the loss by 0.8395. A tenfold larger model buys about a 16% lower loss under this law.

screens.title: A floor bends the line
screens.prose: Text has an irreducible loss $E$ no model can beat. A law with a floor, $L = E + aN^{-\alpha}$, approaches $E$ instead of 0, so in log space it bends towards a flat line.
screens.question: With the floor $E$ known, which fit recovers $\alpha$?

options.text: Fit $\ln(L - E)$ against $\ln N$
Fit $\ln L$ against $\ln N$ as before
options.why: The floor bends that line, so its slope changes along the range.

options.text: Fit $L$ against $\ln N$
options.why: That is still bent by the floor.

options.text: Fit $E$ alone
options.why: $E$ is the flat part; $\alpha$ governs how fast the loss reaches it.

hints.text: Which quantity follows a pure power law?

feedback.correct: $L - E = aN^{-\alpha}$ is a pure power law, a line in log space.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Remove the floor first.

explain.text: Subtract the floor, then fit the line. $E$ must come first, from the flattening of the largest runs, which is why fitted floors are uncertain.

screens.title: Two points
screens.prose: Two models: $10^7$ parameters at loss 3.0 and $10^9$ at loss 2.4.
screens.question: What do two points tell you about a power law?

options.text: They fix $a$ and $\alpha$, and test nothing
They show the losses follow a power law
options.why: Any two points with falling loss fit some power law exactly.

options.text: Nothing: two points cannot fix a line
options.why: Two points fix a line, here in log space.

options.text: They reveal the floor $E$
options.why: A floor needs curvature, which two points cannot show.

hints.text: Two equations, two unknowns, no test.

feedback.correct: Two points always fit exactly; a third point is the first test of the law.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Can two points ever fail to fit?

explain.text: Two unknowns, two points: a perfect fit is guaranteed and proves nothing. Scaling papers fit many runs over many decades for that reason.

screens.title: Power laws in log space
screens.prose:
For $L = aN^{-\alpha}$:
$$\ln L = \ln a - \alpha \ln N$$
Fit the line by least squares on the logs; $\alpha$ is minus the slope and $a$ is $e^{\text{intercept}}$. Each tenfold in $N$ multiplies $L$ by $10^{-\alpha}$.
screens.question: A fit gives slope $-0.2$ in log space. By what factor does the loss shrink when $N$ grows 100 times?

options.why: The law multiplies, it does not subtract.
That is one tenfold; 100 times is two.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Raise 100 to the power $-0.2$.

explain.text: A hundredfold is two tenfolds: $(10^{-0.2})^2 \approx 0.398$. The loss falls by 60%.

screens.title: Market impact
screens.prose: A desk models the cost of a trade of size $Q$ as $\text{cost} = cQ^{\beta}$. Its fills show 2 basis points for a $10^4$-share order and 20 basis points for a $10^6$-share order.
screens.question: What exponent $\beta$ do the two fills give? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the change in log cost by the change in log size.

byKey.one: That would make cost proportional to size: 200 basis points at $10^6$.
byKey.ratio: That is the ratio of costs over the ratio of sizes. Take logs first.

explain.text: $\beta = 0.5$, the square-root impact law, fitted exactly as a scaling law. With only two fills it is a fit, not a test: more order sizes check it.

ideas: $L = aN^{-\alpha}$ is a straight line in $(\ln N, \ln L)$: fit it by least squares on the logs; $\alpha$ is minus the slope.
A floor $E$ bends the line (fit $\ln(L - E)$); two points always fit; extrapolation far past the data is a guess.

formula.name: A power law in log space

summary.trap: Fitting a straight line to $L$ against $N$ on linear axes.

quiz.question: A law has $\alpha = 0.05$. By what factor does the loss shrink per tenfold? Give 4 decimal places.
A law fitted on models from $10^6$ to $10^9$ parameters predicts the loss at $10^{13}$. Why distrust it?

options.text: It is four decades past the data
Nothing: a power law holds at every size
options.why: A floor makes the true curve flatten; the fit cannot know where.

options.text: Because of noise in the fit
options.why: Noise matters, but the larger risk is the untested range.

feedback.correct: Beyond the fitted range the law is a guess; floors bend real curves.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What does the fit know about $10^{13}$?

explain.text: A fit says nothing about sizes it never saw. Kaplan's and Chinchilla's laws differ most where they extrapolate.

quiz.question: In log space a fit gives intercept 1.5 and slope $-0.3$. What are $a$ and $\alpha$?

options.why: The intercept is $\ln a$, and $\alpha$ is minus the slope.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Exponentiate the intercept; negate the slope.

explain.text: The intercept is $\ln a$; the slope is $-\alpha$.
